proofs.proof_tex:
We give an explicit regular-submodel certificate.  A procedure that is uniformly valid over the categorical-instrument model must in particular be valid on every admissible submodel described below.  Take one stratum \(\mathcal X=\{x\}\), take \(\mathcal Z=\mathcal A=\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\), and let \(Z\) be uniform on \(\mathcal Z\).  This design obeys Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}stratum\text{-}instrument\text{-}support}\) whenever the corresponding support-restricted class is nonempty, because then \(K\pi_{\min}\leq1\).  For every \(\tau\in(-1/8,1/8)\), set
\[
 m_0(\tau)=\tfrac12,\qquad
 m_1(\tau)=\tfrac12+\tau,\qquad
 m_a(\tau)=\tfrac14\quad(2\leq a<K).
\]
Independently of \(Z\), draw the binary coordinates \(Y(a)\) independently with \(\Pr\{Y(a)=1\}=m_a(\tau)\), set \(A(z)=z\) for every \(z\), and define the observables by \(A=A(Z)\) and \(Y=Y(A)\).  Independence of \(Z\) from the entire response type verifies Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}instrument\text{-}randomization}\); the two displayed observation equations verify Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass{:}treatment\text{-}consistency}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}outcome\text{-}exclusion}\).  The resulting finite response-type distribution is a member of the fiber, so compatibility holds.

The observable map sends this structural law to the law \(P_\tau\) of \(O=(X,Z,A,Y)\), whose conditional table is
\[
 p_{xzay}(\tau)=\mathbf 1\{a=z\}
 m_z(\tau)^y\{1-m_z(\tau)\}^{1-y}.
\]
The unobserved causal target in stratum \(x\) is the \(K\)-vector \(\theta_x=(E\{Y(a)\mid X=x\})_{a\in\mathcal A}\in[0,1]^K\).  Its identified set under the maintained response-type restrictions is
\[
 \Theta_I(P_\tau)
 =\{Cw:w\in\mathcal W_x(p_x(\tau))\}
 =\mathcal M_x(p_x(\tau)).
\]
We now compute this set rather than imposing its value.  This is the nonnegative response-type projection step.  For any \(w\in\mathcal W_x(p_x(\tau))\), every observed cell with \(A\neq Z\) has probability zero.  Since every coordinate of \(w\) is nonnegative, the response-fiber equalities imply
\[
 w_r>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_r(z)=z
 \quad\text{for every }z\in\mathcal Z.
\]
For each \(a\in\mathcal A\), the equality for the observed cell \((Z,A,Y)=(a,a,1)\) then gives
\[
 (Cw)_a=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}w_r y_r(a)
 =P_\tau(Y=1\mid Z=a)=m_a(\tau).
\]
Thus every compatible response law has the same action-mean vector, and the constructed response law shows attainability.  By Definitions \(\mathrm{def{:}response\text{-}fiber}\) and \(\mathrm{def{:}action\text{-}mean\text{-}polytope}\),
\[
 \mathcal M_x(p_x(\tau))=\{m(\tau)\}.
\]
This proves the link between the causal action means and the observed-law identified set; it is not imposed by definition.

The optimization step uses simplex extreme-point algebra.  For a singleton identified set, Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}joint\text{-}saddle}\) yields, for every \(q\in\Delta_K\),
\[
 R_x(q,p_x(\tau))
 =\max_{b\in\mathcal A}(e_b-q)^\top m(\tau)
 =\max_{b\in\mathcal A}m_b(\tau)-q^\top m(\tau).
\]
Because a linear functional on \(\Delta_K\) is maximized exactly by mixtures supported on its maximizing coordinates, it follows directly that
\[
 Q_x^*(p_x(0))=\operatorname{conv}\{e_0,e_1\},\qquad
 Q_x^*(p_x(\tau))=\{e_1\}\quad(\tau>0),
\]
and \(Q_x^*(p_x(\tau))=\{e_0\}\) for \(\tau<0\).  Hence \(\tau=0\) is a codimension-one intersection of optimal faces and a perturbation of either sign selects a different endpoint.

The impossibility step is an explicit two-law likelihood and total-variation comparison.  Let \(\widehat S_n\) be any data-based random closed-set estimator of the correspondence.  If its Hausdorff or support-function distance from a nonempty compact subset of \(\Delta_K\) is not finite, the asserted contraction already fails; hence it suffices to consider the case in which the relevant realized sets are nonempty and compact.  For a nonempty compact set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^K\), write \(h_S(u)=\sup_{s\in S}u^\top s\).  Suppose that the procedure has asymptotic containment coverage at least \(1-\alpha\), uniformly along all \(n^{-1/2}\)-local sequences through the preceding face intersection.  The constant sequence \(P_0\) is among those sequences, so
\[
 P_0^n\!\left\{\operatorname{conv}\{e_0,e_1\}\subseteq\widehat S_n\right\}
 \geq 1-\alpha-o(1).
\]

Fix \(c>0\) and put \(\tau_n=c/\sqrt n\).  The two affected entries of \(p_x(\tau_n)-p_x(0)\) are \(\tau_n\) and \(-\tau_n\), so this is an \(n^{-1/2}\)-local sequence.  For all sufficiently large \(n\), \(|\tau_n|<1/8\).  Write \(L_\tau=dP_\tau/dP_0\).  The likelihood ratio equals \(1+2\tau\) in the cell \((Z,A,Y)=(1,1,1)\), equals \(1-2\tau\) in the cell \((1,1,0)\), and equals one in every other cell.  Each of the two exceptional cells has \(P_0\)-probability \(1/(2K)\); therefore
\[
 E_0(L_\tau-1)^2
 =2\frac1{2K}(2\tau)^2
 =\frac{4\tau^2}{K}.
\]
For the product likelihood ratio \(L_{\tau_n}^{(n)}=\prod_{i=1}^nL_{\tau_n}(O_i)\), Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}iid\text{-}sampling}\) and \(E_0L_{\tau_n}=1\) give
\[
 E_0\!\left(L_{\tau_n}^{(n)}-1\right)^2
 =\left(1+\frac{4\tau_n^2}{K}\right)^n-1
 \leq \exp(4c^2/K)-1.
\]
Consequently, direct application of \(E|V|\leq(EV^2)^{1/2}\) to the likelihood-ratio formula for total variation gives
\[
 \lVert P_{\tau_n}^n-P_0^n\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \leq \rho_K(c):=\frac12\sqrt{\exp(4c^2/K)-1},
 \qquad \rho_K(c)\longrightarrow0\quad(c\downarrow0).
\]
Choose \(c\) so small that \(\rho_K(c)<1-\alpha\).  Transferring the preceding coverage event across this total-variation bound yields
\[
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}P_{\tau_n}^n\{e_0\in\widehat S_n\}
 \geq 1-\alpha-\rho_K(c)>0.
\]

Under \(P_{\tau_n}\), however, the true optimizer correspondence is \(\{e_1\}\).  On the event \(e_0\in\widehat S_n\),
\[
 d_{\mathrm H}(\widehat S_n,\{e_1\})
 \geq\lVert e_0-e_1\rVert_2=\sqrt2.
\]
For the support-function distance, take \(u=(e_0-e_1)/\sqrt2\).  Then \(\lVert u\rVert_2=1\) and, on the same event,
\[
 h_{\widehat S_n}(u)-h_{\{e_1\}}(u)
 \geq u^\top(e_0-e_1)=\sqrt2.
\]
Thus, under the local sequence \(P_{\tau_n}\), either distance is bounded below by a fixed positive constant with probability bounded away from zero.  In particular, \(\sqrt n\) times either distance is not tight, so uniform \(n^{-1/2}\)-contraction is impossible.  The argument treated \(\widehat S_n\) as arbitrary and therefore applies to \(\mathfrak H_{\mathrm{face}}\) as well; no choice of a population face was supplied.

Finally, the fallback step uses exact confidence-set inversion.  This lower-bound argument does not contradict the finite-sample fallback.  The already-established Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}cp\text{-}correspondence\text{-}coverage}\) gives uniform containment coverage for the confidence-fiber union, including at face intersections.  The calculation above shows precisely why such an honest set may have to retain locally indistinguishable faces and therefore cannot also be required to contract uniformly at the \(n^{-1/2}\) rate to the exact optimizer correspondence.

prose_updates.tldr: For the binary-outcome, finite-stratum specialization of Song et al.'s model M1, the paper identifies the full joint action-mean polytope and solves the resulting randomized minimax-regret game. Its inferential conclusion is a sharp regular--irregular dichotomy: on separated nondegenerate unique faces, the moving-coefficient KKT map is Hadamard differentiable and admits a uniform root-\(n\) Gaussian law; at intersections of optimal faces, no uniformly honest random closed set can also contract at the root-\(n\) rate to the exact optimizer correspondence. The exact Bonferroni Clopper--Pearson confidence-fiber union remains uniformly valid at those intersections, but it is deliberately noncontracting there. Pure-rule certificates, the spike-state specialization, the exact three-action joint-versus-rectangle witness, and deployed-regret certification complete the decision analysis.

project_justification.gap: Song et al.'s model M1 supplies the compatible response-law restrictions for discrete instruments and outcomes, but it does not provide randomized minimax-regret optimization or sampling inference for the resulting optimizer correspondence. Existing random-linear-program theory generally fixes constraint normals, while here the observable multinomial table changes both the feasible response bases and the active regret coefficients. The unresolved inferential issue was therefore not merely differentiability on a regular face, but whether honest root-\(n\) contraction can survive intersections of optimal faces.
project_justification.niche: The paper studies the binary-outcome, finite-covariate-stratum specialization of Song et al.'s M1 and links response-type partial identification to a finite randomized saddle program. It separates regular laws, where observable basis, slack, reduced-cost, and active-face margins stabilize the KKT system, from irregular face intersections, where locally indistinguishable laws have optimizer correspondences separated by a fixed distance.
project_justification.fill: The positive result gives the explicit moving-coefficient derivative and uniform Gaussian policy-and-value law on separated nondegenerate unique faces. The negative result gives an explicit full-compliance local submodel proving that no data-based random closed set can combine uniform asymptotic coverage with root-\(n\) contraction at face intersections. Exact finite-sample confidence-fiber coverage is the valid noncontracting fallback. The rectangle-safety counterexample also applies to Hruza et al.'s broader overlapping bound-agnostic class by inclusion, but the positive sampling and KKT theorem is proved only for this paper's narrower response-type model and does not transfer by that inclusion.

prose_updates.related_work: Manski2000TreatmentChoice separates treatment choice from point identification, and Stoye2007ManyTreatments supplies the spike-state population allocation benchmark recovered here when every spike is feasible. Masten2023ManyTreatmentRules and MontielOleaQiuStoye2026Asymptotics analyze different repeated-sample or local-Gaussian treatment-choice problems, whereas this paper studies fixed-law inference for a population mixed-action optimizer under partial identification. Cui2021PartialIDDecisions randomizes a binary action from marginal contrast bounds; it does not optimize three or more actions against a joint categorical-instrument response polytope. SongEtAl2026CategoricalIV supplies model M1's response-law compatibility restrictions; the present model is its binary-outcome, finite-stratum specialization, not a claim about all of models M1--M5. SachsEtAl2023SymbolicBounds and MastinJailletChin2014RandomizedRegret provide the response-function linear-program and finite saddle ingredients, whose composition is treated as background. HruzaEtAl2026CategoricalPIL studies a broader, overlapping bound-agnostic class and a coordinatewise-interval decision rule. Inclusion carries the paper's negative rectangle-safety witness to that broader class, but it does not carry the positive response-basis, KKT, or Gaussian theorem. BonnansShapiro2000Perturbation informs the separated-face analysis; KlattMunkZemel2022RandomLP and LiuBuneaNilesWeed2023LPConfidence concern fixed-coefficient formulations that do not cover the moving active normals here. FangSantos2019DirectionalInference motivates derivative-aware inference at nonsmooth maps, while the theorem here proves the stronger obstruction that uniformly honest root-\(n\) contraction to the exact optimizer set is impossible at face intersections. ClopperPearson1934Binomial and ChernozhukovHongTamer2007Sets inform the exact, noncontracting confidence-fiber fallback.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The Gaussian policy-and-regret law is restricted to the observable nondegenerate unique-face class with fixed-support, response-basis, rank, slack, reduced-cost, and active-weight margins. At face intersections, the impossibility theorem rules out uniformly honest root-\(n\) contraction to the exact optimizer correspondence; the Bonferroni confidence-fiber union remains valid but can be conservative and noncontracting. The negative rectangle-safety witness transfers to broader classes containing the displayed law, including the overlapping Hruza et al. class, but the positive active-basis and KKT theory requires this paper's response-type structure and stated margins.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The maintained causal model is the binary-outcome, finite-stratum specialization of Song et al.'s model M1, with finite randomized instrument support, categorical treatment, response-type exogeneity, consistency, exclusion, positive stratum--instrument support, and response-fiber compatibility. The response-function projection and its composition with a finite randomized-regret linear program are background ingredients. Uniform root-\(n\) Gaussian inference is proved only on the separated nondegenerate unique-face class; it is not claimed at face intersections. At those intersections, an explicit local submodel proves that every uniformly honest random closed set must forgo root-\(n\) contraction to the exact optimizer correspondence unless a population face is selected or the target is weakened to a local outer limit. The exact Bonferroni Clopper--Pearson confidence-fiber set remains finite-sample valid without a contraction claim. Hruza et al.'s class is broader and overlapping rather than identical: only the negative rectangle-safety counterexample transfers upward by inclusion, while the positive sampling and KKT theorem does not.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix a stratum \(x\) and \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\in\mathfrak P_{\kappa,\varepsilon}\).  All norms below are Euclidean or their induced operator norms.  The fixed-support multinomial tangent space at \(p_x\) is
\[
 \mathcal T_x
 =\left\{h:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A,\,y\in\{0,1\}}h_{zay}=0
       \text{ for every }z,\quad
       h_{zay}=0\text{ if }p_{xzay}=0\right\}.
\]
We prove the deterministic stability, differentiability, geometric obstruction, and stochastic conclusions in turn.

First consider the response bases.  Let \(r_B=\operatorname{rank}(\widetilde B)\), let \(\mathfrak B\) be the finite collection of \(r_B\)-element sets \(\beta\subseteq\mathcal R\) for which \(\widetilde B_\beta\) is nonsingular, and put
\[
 w_\beta(p_x)=\widetilde B_\beta^{-1}\widetilde p_x.
\]
The appended normalization coordinate in \(\widetilde p_x\) is constant, so, for a fixed matrix \(D_\beta\),
\[
 w_\beta(p_x+h)-w_\beta(p_x)=D_\beta h.
 \tag{1}
\]
There are finitely many \(\beta\), and hence
\[
 L_B:=\max_{\beta\in\mathfrak B}\|D_\beta\|<\infty.
 \tag{2}
\]
The response-fiber compatibility assumption ensures that the standard-form polytope \(\mathcal W_x(p_x)\) is nonempty.  It has a basic feasible point: indeed, choose a feasible \(w\) with support of minimum cardinality.  If the columns of \(\widetilde B\) on that support were linearly dependent, a nonzero vector in their null space would have both signs because the last row of \(\widetilde B\) is \(\mathbf 1^\top\); moving in one of its two directions until a positive coordinate first reached zero would preserve feasibility and strictly reduce the support.  Thus those columns are independent.  Extending them to \(r_B\) independent columns, if necessary, gives a nonsingular \(\widetilde B_\beta\) whose basic solution is nonnegative.  Consequently \(\mathcal B_x(p_x)\neq\varnothing\).

By the response-basis roster margin, for every \(\beta\in\mathfrak B\) and every coordinate \(j\),
\[
 |w_{\beta,j}(p_x)|\geq\kappa.
 \tag{3}
\]
Equations (1)--(3) imply that, whenever \(h\in\mathcal T_x\) and
\[
 \|h\|<\rho_B:=\frac{\kappa}{2\max\{L_B,1\}},
 \tag{4}
\]
every coordinate of every basic solution retains its sign.  Hence
\[
 \mathcal B_x(p_x+h)=\mathcal B_x(p_x).
 \tag{5}
\]
In particular, a basis feasible at \(p_x\) remains feasible, so the perturbed response fiber remains nonempty.  This explicitly uses compatibility for existence, nonsingularity for inversion, and the positive margin \(\kappa\) before division in (4).  Since \(K\), \(\mathcal Z\), and \(\mathcal R\) are finite and \(\widetilde B\) is fixed, \(\rho_B\) is uniform over the asserted class.

On the roster in (5), every row of the regret matrix is affine:
\[
 G_{(b,\beta),a}(p_x+h)
 =G_{(b,\beta),a}(p_x)
  +(e_b-e_a)^\top C_\beta D_\beta h.
 \tag{6}
\]
Thus all norms of \(G_x\) and all derivatives in (6) are bounded by constants depending only on the fixed finite matrices.  Let
\[
 \mathcal I=\mathcal I_x(p_x),\quad
 \mathcal J=\mathcal J_x(p_x),\quad
 H=H_x(p_x),\quad u=u_x(p_x),
\]
and, on this fixed roster, write
\[
 H_h=H_x(p_x+h),\quad \Delta_h=H_h-H.
\]
Equation (6) gives a uniform constant \(L_H<\infty\) such that
\[
 \|\Delta_h\|\leq L_H\|h\|.
 \tag{7}
\]
The active-system rank assumption states \(\sigma_{\min}(H)\geq\kappa>0\).  Therefore, if \(L_H\|h\|\leq\kappa/2\), the elementary inequality
\[
 \|H_h z\|\geq\|Hz\|-\|\Delta_hz\|
 \geq(\kappa-L_H\|h\|)\|z\|
\]
shows that
\[
 H_h^{-1}\text{ exists},\quad \|H_h^{-1}\|\leq 2\kappa^{-1}.
 \tag{8}
\]
Because the active right-hand side is constant, define the candidate
\[
 u_h:=H_h^{-1}g_x(p_x).
 \tag{9}
\]
The resolvent identity and (7)--(9) give
\[
 u_h-u=-H_h^{-1}\Delta_hu,\quad
 \|u_h-u\|\leq2\kappa^{-1}L_H\|u\|\,\|h\|.
 \tag{10}
\]
The vector \(u\) is uniformly bounded.  Its \(q\)- and \(\lambda\)-blocks belong to simplices; feasible basic response laws give action means in \([0,1]\), so every entry of \(G_x\) lies in \([-1,1]\); hence \(|v_x|\leq1\), and active stationarity gives \(\eta_x=G_{\cdot,a}^\top\lambda\in[-1,1]\) for any \(a\in\mathcal J\).  The dimensions take only finitely many values.

We now verify rather than assume that (9) remains the full saddle solution.  By the active-weight margin and (10), after reducing a common neighborhood if needed,
\[
 q_{h,a}\geq\kappa/2\quad(a\in\mathcal J),
 \quad
 \lambda_{h,s}\geq\kappa/2\quad(s\in\mathcal I).
 \tag{11}
\]
The primal-slack and reduced-cost margins, together with (6) and (10), similarly imply
\[
 v_h-G_{s,\cdot}(p_x+h)q_h\geq\kappa/2
       \quad(s\notin\mathcal I),
 \tag{12}
\]
and
\[
 G_{\cdot,a}(p_x+h)^\top\lambda_h-\eta_h\geq\kappa/2
       \quad(a\notin\mathcal J).
 \tag{13}
\]
The equations \(H_hu_h=g_x(p_x)\) are, row by row,
\[
 G_{\mathcal I,\mathcal J}(p_x+h)q_{h,\mathcal J}
       =v_h\mathbf 1_{\mathcal I},
 \quad
 G_{\mathcal I,\mathcal J}(p_x+h)^\top\lambda_{h,\mathcal I}
       =\eta_h\mathbf 1_{\mathcal J},
 \quad
 \mathbf 1^\top q_h=1,
 \quad
 \mathbf 1^\top\lambda_h=1.
 \tag{14}
\]
Extend \(q_h\) and \(\lambda_h\) by zero outside \(\mathcal J\) and \(\mathcal I\).  Equations (11)--(14) are precisely primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness.  More explicitly, (14) yields
\[
 v_h
 =\sum_s\lambda_{h,s}v_h
 =\sum_s\lambda_{h,s}G_{s,\cdot}(p_x+h)q_h
 =q_h^\top G_x(p_x+h)^\top\lambda_h
 =\eta_h.
 \tag{15}
\]
For every other feasible \((q',t')\), (13)--(15) give weak duality directly:
\[
 t'\geq\sum_s\lambda_{h,s}G_{s,\cdot}(p_x+h)q'
 =(q')^\top G_x(p_x+h)^\top\lambda_h
 \geq\eta_h\mathbf 1^\top q'=v_h.
 \tag{16}
\]
Thus (9) is optimal.

It is also the unique primal--dual optimum.  Equality in (16) for another primal optimum forces every row in \(\mathcal I\) to bind by (11), and forces \(q'_a=0\) for every \(a\notin\mathcal J\) by (13).  Keeping the candidate dual block fixed, \((q'_{\mathcal J},t',\lambda_{h,\mathcal I},\eta_h)\) then solves the square system (14), so (8) implies \((q',t')=(q_h,v_h)\).  Conversely, complementary slackness with (12) forces every dual optimum to put zero weight outside \(\mathcal I\), while (11) forces stationarity equality on \(\mathcal J\); keeping the candidate primal block fixed again produces (14), and (8) gives uniqueness of the dual block.  We have proved
\[
 \mathcal I_x(p_x+h)=\mathcal I,\quad
 \mathcal J_x(p_x+h)=\mathcal J.
 \tag{17}
\]
All radii used in (11)--(13) can be chosen uniformly: there are finitely many rosters and active-set pairs, (6) has finitely many fixed derivatives, (8) is controlled by the common \(\kappa\), the four relevant positivity and slack quantities are bounded below by the same \(\kappa\), and \(u\) is uniformly bounded.  Together with (5), this proves the claimed uniform local constancy and the unique active-system representation.

We next differentiate that representation.  On the neighborhood just obtained, \(E_x(p_x+h)=E_x(p_x)=:E\), \(g_x(p_x+h)=g_x(p_x)=:g\), and \(H_x\) is affine.  Thus \(\Delta_h=DH_x(p_x)[h]\).  The identities \(H_hu_h=g=Hu\) imply
\[
 u_h-u=-H^{-1}\Delta_hu_h.
\]
Consequently
\[
 u_h-u+H^{-1}\Delta_hu
 =-H^{-1}\Delta_h(u_h-u),
\]
and (7), (8), and (10) yield a uniform constant \(C<\infty\) such that
\[
 \left\|u_h-u+H^{-1}DH_x(p_x)[h]u\right\|
 \leq C\|h\|^2.
 \tag{18}
\]
Since \(T_x(p_x)=Eu_x(p_x)\), (18) proves Hadamard differentiability tangentially to \(\mathcal T_x\), including along every sequence \(h_m\to h\) in that tangent space, with derivative
\[
 DT_x(p_x)[h]
 =-E_x(p_x)H_x(p_x)^{-1}DH_x(p_x)[h]u_x(p_x)
 =J_x(p_x)[h].
 \tag{19}
\]
This also proves explicitly that the right-hand side is constant on the face and that all parameter dependence of the active equations occurs through \(G_{\mathcal I,\mathcal J}(p_x)\) in \(H_x(p_x)\).

We turn to the facet-normal assertion.  Work in one fixed-support cell on which the roster and the active sets are fixed.  For \(s=(b,\beta)\), let
\[
 m_\beta(p_x)=C_\beta\widetilde B_\beta^{-1}\widetilde p_x.
\]
Then
\[
 G_{s,a}(p_x)=m_{\beta,b}(p_x)-m_{\beta,a}(p_x),
 \quad G_{s,b}(p_x)=0,
 \tag{20}
\]
and \(a_{x,s}(p_x)=(G_{s,\cdot}(p_x)^\top,-1)^\top\) is affine.  If
\[
 (I-\bar a_{x,s}\bar a_{x,s}^\top)Da_{x,s}(p_x)[h]=0,
\]
then \(Da_{x,s}(p_x)[h]=c,a_{x,s}(p_x)\) for some scalar \(c\).  The last coordinate on the left is zero, whereas the last coordinate of \(a_{x,s}\) is \(-1\); hence \(c=0\) and
\[
 (I-\bar a_{x,s}\bar a_{x,s}^\top)Da_{x,s}(p_x)[h]=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 Da_{x,s}(p_x)[h]=0.
 \tag{21}
\]
It follows from the definition of \(\omega_x\) and (21) that \(\omega_x(p_x)=0\) exactly when every active normal has zero derivative in every unit tangent direction.  Those derivatives are constant on the cell because (20) is affine.  Therefore either all active normals are locally constant, which is stronger than constancy up to positive scale, or \(\omega_x\) is nowhere zero on that cell.  In the second case its zero set is empty, hence is the proper algebraic subset defined, for example, by the polynomial equation \(1=0\).  This proves the stated algebraic dichotomy.

For completeness, we now handle the affine-hull issue in the fixed-left-hand-side obstruction.  An active scenario inequality carrying positive unique dual weight cannot be redundant.  To see this, suppose row \(s\) were implied by the other scenario inequalities, the inequalities \(-q_a\leq0\), and \(\mathbf 1^\top q=1\).  Finite linear elimination gives nonnegative \(\rho_r\) and \(\gamma_a\), and a scalar \(\nu\leq0\), such that
\[
 a_{x,s}
 =\sum_{r\ne s}\rho_r a_{x,r}
   -\sum_a\gamma_a(e_a,0)+\nu(\mathbf 1,0).
 \tag{22}
\]
This multiplier identity follows directly by separating \(a_{x,s}\) from the finitely generated cone on the right: a separating vector, if it existed, would satisfy every retained inequality and the simplex equality but violate row \(s\), contradicting redundancy.  Evaluate (22) at the optimum, where row \(s\) is tight.  Every term on the right is nonpositive, so each term with a positive multiplier is tight and \(\nu=0\).  Comparing last coordinates gives \(\sum_{r\ne s}\rho_r=1\).  If \(c=G_x^\top\lambda-\eta\mathbf 1\geq0\) is the vector of dual slacks, replace
\[
 \lambda_s\text{ by }0,\quad
 \lambda_r\text{ by }\lambda_r+\lambda_s\rho_r\quad(r\ne s),
 \quad
 c\text{ by }c+\lambda_s\gamma.
 \tag{23}
\]
Equations (22)--(23) preserve dual feasibility, \(\mathbf 1^\top\lambda=1\), and the dual objective, but change the dual solution because \(\lambda_s>0\).  This contradicts the unique-primal--dual-face assumption.  Hence every row in \(\mathcal I\) survives removal of redundant inequalities.  The epigraph has nonempty relative interior in \(\mathbf 1^\top q=1\): take \(q_a>0\) for all \(a\) and take \(t\) strictly larger than every \(G_{s,\cdot}q\).  In a finite inequality description of a polyhedron with nonempty relative interior, a nonredundant row cuts a facet.  Indeed, after deleting that row there is a point satisfying all retained inequalities but violating it; the segment from this point to the displayed strict interior point first meets the deleted row at a point where every retained inequality is strict, producing a relatively open subset of the row's hyperplane.  Thus every row in \(\mathcal I\) defines a facet of the epigraph relative to that affine hull.

Suppose, contrary to the theorem, that a neighborhood of a point with \(\omega_x(p_x)>0\) had an irredundant epigraph representation whose left-hand coefficient matrix was fixed and whose dependence on \(p_x\) appeared only in the right-hand side.  Two inequalities defining the same facet relative to \(\mathbf 1^\top q=1\) have positively proportional linear parts modulo a multiple of \((\mathbf 1,0)\): their restrictions to the direction space \(\{(d_q,d_t):\mathbf 1^\top d_q=0\}\) are nonzero linear functionals with the same codimension-one kernel and the same feasible side.  Because the fixed representation has finitely many rows and \(a_{x,s}(p_x)\) varies continuously, each active facet has locally a fixed matching row.  After normalizing that row's \(t\)-coefficient to \(-1\), facet equality therefore gives
\[
 a_{x,s}(p')=(d_s^\top,-1)^\top+c_s(p')(\mathbf 1,0)
 \tag{24}
\]
throughout a smaller neighborhood.  The scale in (24) is constant because the last coordinate of \(a_{x,s}\) is always \(-1\).  Finally, (20) gives \(G_{s,b}(p')=0\) for every \(p'\), so the \(b\)-th coordinate of (24) yields \(c_s(p')=-d_{s,b}\), also constant.  Thus every active \(a_{x,s}(p')\) is locally constant, contradicting \(\omega_x(p_x)>0\) by (21).  This proves that coefficient motion cannot be transferred entirely to right-hand sides in the original \((q,t)\)-coordinates.

It remains to prove the two uniform stochastic assertions.  Define
\[
 \widehat\pi_{xz}=\frac{N_{xz}}n,
 \quad
 \psi_{x,z,a,y}(O_i)
 =\frac{\mathbf 1\{X_i=x,Z_i=z\}}{\pi_{xz}}
  \left(\mathbf 1\{A_i=a,Y_i=y\}-p_{xzay}\right).
 \tag{25}
\]
The support assumption \(\pi_{xz}\geq\pi_{\min}>0\) justifies division in (25), and
\[
 E_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}}\psi_x(O_i)=0,
 \quad
 \|\psi_x(O_i)\|\leq C_\psi\pi_{\min}^{-1}
 \tag{26}
\]
for a constant \(C_\psi\) depending only on the fixed alphabet.  Put
\[
 S_{xzay,n}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
 \mathbf 1\{X_i=x,Z_i=z\}
 \left(\mathbf 1\{A_i=a,Y_i=y\}-p_{xzay}\right).
\]
On \(N_{xz}>0\), the ratio identity is exact:
\[
 \widehat p_{xzay}-p_{xzay}
 =\frac{S_{xzay,n}}{\widehat\pi_{xz}}
 =\frac{S_{xzay,n}}{\pi_{xz}}
  +\frac{S_{xzay,n}(\pi_{xz}-\widehat\pi_{xz})}
         {\pi_{xz}\widehat\pi_{xz}}.
 \tag{27}
\]
Under independent sampling, the two centered quantities in the numerator of the remainder in (27) have variances at most \(n^{-1}\).  Chebyshev's inequality therefore gives, uniformly in \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\),
\[
 S_{xzay,n}=O_P(n^{-1/2}),\quad
 \widehat\pi_{xz}-\pi_{xz}=O_P(n^{-1/2}).
 \tag{28}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \sup_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}}
 P_{\mathrm{obs}}\!\left(\widehat\pi_{xz}<\frac{\pi_{xz}}2\right)
 \leq \frac{4}{n\pi_{\min}^2}\longrightarrow0,
 \quad
 P_{\mathrm{obs}}(N_{xz}=0)
 =(1-\pi_{xz})^n\leq e^{-n\pi_{\min}}.
 \tag{29}
\]
On the first event complementary to (29), the absolute remainder in (27) is at most
\[
 2\pi_{\min}^{-2}|S_{xzay,n}|\,
       |\widehat\pi_{xz}-\pi_{xz}|.
\]
The product of the two uniform \(O_P(n^{-1/2})\) quantities in (28) is uniformly \(O_P(n^{-1})\), as follows directly by intersecting the two events on which their root-\(n\) magnitudes are at most a fixed \(M\).  Since the number of cells is finite, (25)--(29) prove
\[
 \widehat p_x-p_x
 =\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_x(O_i)+r_{x,n},
 \quad
 \sup_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}\in\mathfrak P_{\kappa,\varepsilon}}
 P_{\mathrm{obs}}\!\left(\sqrt n\|r_{x,n}\|>\delta\right)
 \longrightarrow0
 \tag{30}
\]
for every \(\delta>0\).  The same variance bounds imply \(\widehat p_x-p_x=O_P(n^{-1/2})\) uniformly.

True zero cells remain zero almost surely, and every positive cell is at least \(\varepsilon\) by the fixed-cell-support assumption.  Equations (4), (17), (29), and (30) therefore imply that \(\widehat p_x\) lies in the same fixed-support compatible active cell with probability tending to one uniformly.  On the exceptional event, which has uniformly vanishing probability, take any fixed measurable extension of the local active-system map; this convention cannot affect either asserted asymptotic statement.  Applying the uniform quadratic remainder (18) to \(h=\widehat p_x-p_x\), and then using (30), gives
\[
 \sqrt n\{T_x(\widehat p_x)-T_x(p_x)\}
 =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nJ_x(p_x)\psi_x(O_i)+o_P(1)
 \tag{31}
\]
uniformly over \(\mathfrak P_{\kappa,\varepsilon}\).  Indeed, the linear contribution of \(r_{x,n}\) is uniformly \(o_P(1)\), while
\[
 \sqrt n\,\|\widehat p_x-p_x\|^2=o_P(1)
\]
uniformly.  Equation (31) is exactly the first displayed probability limit in the theorem.

Finally, (8), the finite collection of derivatives in (6), and the uniform bound on \(u_x\) show from (19) that
\[
 \sup_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}\in\mathfrak P_{\kappa,\varepsilon}}
 \|J_x(p_x)\|<\infty.
 \tag{32}
\]
The random vector
\[
 \xi_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}}(O_i)=J_x(p_x)\psi_x(O_i)
\]
has mean zero by (26), ranges over the fixed finite alphabet \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z\times\mathcal A\times\{0,1\}\), and is uniformly bounded by (26) and (32).  Its covariance is
\[
 E\{\xi_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}}(O_i)\xi_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}}(O_i)^\top\}
 =J_x(p_x)\Sigma_x(p_x)J_x(p_x)^\top.
\]
The already established finite-alphabet uniform central limit lemma therefore yields
\[
 \sup_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}\in\mathfrak P_{\kappa,\varepsilon}}
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\!\left(
 \mathcal L_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}}\!\left(
  \frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nJ_x(p_x)\psi_x(O_i)\right),
 N\!\left(0,J_x(p_x)\Sigma_x(p_x)J_x(p_x)^\top\right)
 \right)\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{33}
\]
That lemma explicitly permits singular covariance matrices.  For any \(\delta>0\), coupling the two random vectors in (31) on their common sample gives a bounded-Lipschitz distance at most \(\delta+2P(\|o_P(1)\|>\delta)\).  Combining this uniform bound with (31), (33), and the triangle inequality proves the claimed uniform Gaussian approximation and completes the proof.
